objectives: Write a subject line that tells the reader what the email is about and gets it opened.
Structure an email so a busy reader gets the point in the first three lines.
Choose the right level of formality for the situation and the person.
Ask for something clearly, with a deadline and a next step.
Apologise in a way that takes responsibility and moves the work forward.
Avoid the six errors that make a professional email look careless.
Reply, attach and file information without making the reader ask twice.

sections.body:
An email is a written conversation. That is its whole problem and its whole advantage. Unlike a phone call, it leaves a record. Unlike a meeting, it can be read in ten seconds by someone who was not in the room.

Professional email is therefore not about being polite in every sentence. It is about making your intention clear to a reader who is busy, slightly distracted, and reading on a phone. The standard is simple: the reader should know what you want, by when, and what they need to do next, without reading the email twice.

Three things separate a professional email from an informal one. First, **structure**: the information appears in a predictable order, so the reader can stop reading as soon as they have what they came for. Second, **register**, the level of formality the situation expects. Third, **precision**: short sentences, specific names, real dates, clear deadlines.

The register question is the one people get wrong most often, and it is not really about grammar. It is about distance. Writing to a client, to a manager you do not know, or to a stranger is formal: full greetings, complete sentences, no contractions. Writing to a close colleague you have worked with for three years can be informal: a first name, a short opening, contractions. The mistake is not being informal with a stranger. The mistake is being *too* formal with your own team, because that reads as distance you did not intend, and it costs you warmth you did not mean to lose.

A third thing distinguishes email from every other written text: it is asynchronous. You will not get an answer in the moment. So an email has to work without the conversation around it. It has to contain its own context, because the reader does not have yesterday's meeting in their head, and they may open it three days later with half a dozen other things on top.

Read this article and you will be able to write emails that get answered quickly, because each of them has a clear subject line, a structure, and a request that names a date.
examples: Subject: Revised quotation for the March delivery, by Friday 14 March
Dear Ms Nguyen,
I am writing to ask whether you can send me the updated figures by Friday 14 March.
Could you please confirm whether this works for you?
sections.heading: What makes an email professional

sections.body:
Every professional email has the same anatomy, whether it is two lines or twenty. Knowing the anatomy means you never have to wonder where to put something.

**1. The subject line.** It is the most important line in the email, because it is often the only one read. It should say what the email is about, in a form the reader can search for later. "Question about the March delivery" is weak. "Revised quotation for the March delivery, by Friday 14 March" tells the reader both the topic and the date that matters. Keep it under about eight words if you can, and never leave it empty.

**2. The greeting.** "Dear Mr Tran," is the safe default for anyone you do not know well or anyone you are writing to formally. "Hi Mai," is normal and friendly for a colleague you work with regularly. "Hello," works widely and slightly carefully. Never greet a client or a stranger with "Hey".

**3. The opening line.** One or two sentences that state why you are writing. Many people skip this and start with background, which makes the reader hunt for the point. Put the point first, then the background. "I am writing to ask for your approval on the revised schedule" is better than "I hope this email finds you well, I wanted to reach out about the schedule we discussed."

**4. The body.** Short paragraphs, one idea each. Three or four sentences is a healthy paragraph. Use a numbered list when there are several separate points or several actions the reader must take, because a list is easier to act on than a paragraph.

**5. The action or the ask.** Say clearly what you want the reader to do, by when. If you need a decision, name the options. If you are sending information and need nothing back, say that too: "No reply is needed, I just wanted to keep you informed." This last line is underused and it prevents a great many unnecessary replies.

**6. The close.** A short sign-off, then your name. "Kind regards," or "Best regards," or "Thanks," are all fine. Add your job title if the reader may not know it. Below the signature, put whatever the reader needs to act: your phone number, a link, the document version.

One more part, optional but professional: a line of **context** under the subject, sometimes called a preamble. "Following our call on 12 March about the Haiphong shipment," tells the reader why this email exists without a paragraph. It is particularly useful when you are writing to someone you do not know.
examples: Subject: Revised quotation for the March delivery, by Friday 14 March
Dear Mr Tran,
Following our call on 12 March, I have attached the revised quotation.
Please let me know if the new delivery date of 28 March works for you.
Kind regards,
Linh Tran, Export Officer
sections.heading: The six parts of a professional email

sections.body:
When a message matters, do not write it in one pass. These steps take ten minutes and remove most of the mistakes.

First, decide the **one thing** you want from the reader. If you have two unrelated requests, send two emails. An email with two purposes gets half an answer.

Second, write the **subject line** before the body. It forces you to decide what the email is about, and it becomes the label for the conversation.

Third, write the **ask** in one sentence, on paper, before you write anything else. "Please confirm by Friday whether you approve the revised schedule." Everything else in the email exists to support that sentence.

Fourth, add the **context** the reader needs, in three or four short paragraphs. Cut anything the reader already knows or can look up.

Fifth, read it **once for content and once for tone**. On the content pass, check that every fact is right: names, dates, numbers, file names, the deadline. On the tone pass, read it as the recipient. Would you be annoyed to receive this? Is anything passive-aggressive, even accidentally?

Sixth, **read the subject line and the first line together** as they will appear in the inbox list. That is what decides whether the email is opened.
examples: Ask: please confirm by Friday whether you approve the revised schedule.
Do not put two different requests in one email.
sections.heading: How to write an email in six steps
steps: Decide the single thing you want the reader to do.
Write the subject line before the body.
Write your request in one sentence.
Add only the context the reader needs.
Read once for facts and once for tone.
Check the subject line and first line as they appear in the inbox.

sections.body:
Register is the level of formality you write at. It is decided by two things: how well you know the reader, and how much is at stake.

**Formal** is right for a first contact with someone you do not know, for a client, for anyone senior to you, for complaints and for anything with legal weight. In formal English you use full greetings, complete sentences, no contractions ("I do not" rather than "I don't"), and you avoid chatty openers. "I would be grateful if you could confirm the position by 20 March." The politeness is in the structure, not in the softness.

**Neutral professional** is the default for colleagues and for most working relationships. Full sentences, contractions allowed, first names. "Could you confirm the position by 20 March?" This is the register most workplace email lives in, and it is the safest choice when you are unsure.

**Informal** is for close colleagues you know well. "Can you get me the numbers by the 20th?" is fine. It is not appropriate for anything you would need to show to a third party.

Two rules of thumb for choosing. First, **match the register you are received in**, not the one you want. If your manager writes to you formally, reply formally. Second, **when in doubt, go one step more formal than feels natural**. Nobody has ever complained that a work email was slightly too polite.

Watch for the other side of the trap. Excessive formality reads as cold, and it can sound sarcastic in some offices: "I would be most grateful if you could find the time to respond at your earliest convenience." Excessive informality in writing reads as carelessness, because written words are permanent and are read by people who were not in the room.

And one cultural note. Business English is the international default for written work, and many professionals write in it even when they speak their first language at home. It is not cold. It is the shared written register of work, and you can be warm inside it: "I hope the week is going well for you" is friendly, and "Looking forward to your reply" is warm.
examples: I would be grateful if you could confirm the position by 20 March.
Could you confirm the position by 20 March?
Can you get me the numbers by the 20th?
I hope the week is going well for you. Looking forward to your reply.
sections.heading: Choosing the register

sections.body:
These are the terms you will meet in office email, and what each one actually means.

**CC** (carbon copy) puts a visible recipient on the email. **BCC** (blind carbon copy) puts a hidden recipient on it. Use BCC for a distribution list when the recipients do not need to see each other, and use CC when they should, so nobody is surprised by who is reading.

An **attachment** is a file sent with the email. A **draft** is an unsent email saved for later. **Reply all** sends the answer to every recipient. **Threading** is the chain of messages with the same subject; replying inside the thread keeps the history, and starting a new thread loses it.

An **action item** is a task that somebody has agreed to do. **Follow-up** is a message sent after the first one, either to remind or to ask for a decision. **Escalation** is taking a matter to someone more senior, and it should be used sparingly. **Turnaround time** is how long a reply is expected to take. **Out of office** is the automatic reply sent when you are away.

**Copy** in the sense of a printed copy is usually written **copier** in British English and **copy** in American English, but as a verb both mean to send someone a copy of a message. **Circulate** means to send a document to a group of people. **Chase** means to follow up on something that is late. **Flag** means to draw attention to a point.

And two words about the writing itself. **Plain English** means writing that a reader understands at first reading, without jargon. **Sign-off** is the closing line and signature. **Courtesy copy** is a copy sent for information only, with no action required, which is why so many people write "for information" at the top of an email.
sections.heading: The words professional email uses, one by one

terms.example: I have copied your manager so that she knows the new date.
terms.gloss: A recipient added to an email and shown to everyone, so all readers can see who else has it.

terms.example: I put the whole branch on BCC so nobody sees the full list.
terms.gloss: A hidden recipient. The other recipients cannot see that this person has been included.

terms.example: Please find the attachment, called Quotation-March-2026.pdf.
terms.gloss: A file sent together with the email. It should be named clearly and referred to in the body.

terms.example: There are two action items: sending the figures and confirming the date.
terms.gloss: A task that a named person has agreed to do. In longer emails these are listed explicitly.

terms.example: This is a short follow-up to my email of last Tuesday.
terms.gloss: A message sent after an earlier one, either to remind someone or to ask for a decision.

terms.example: If we do not hear back by Friday, we will need to escalate this.
terms.gloss: Taking a matter to a more senior person because it has not moved. Use it only when it is genuinely warranted.

terms.example: Our usual turnaround time for quotations is two working days.
terms.gloss: How long a reply is expected to take. Often agreed in advance rather than assumed.

terms.example: You will get an out of office message until 20 April.
terms.gloss: The automatic reply sent while you are away, telling people when you will return and who to contact instead.

terms.example: I circulated the minutes to everyone on the project.
terms.gloss: To send a document to a group of people for information, usually with no action required.

terms.example: Use a plain sign-off: Kind regards, then your name and title.
terms.gloss: The closing line of an email, such as "Kind regards", followed by your name.

sections.body:
Most work email is a request in some form, and most missed requests are requests written badly.

A request needs four things: **what** you want, **who** should do it, **by when**, and **what you will do if nothing happens**. The fourth is optional but it is what turns a wish into a request.

Be specific about the deadline, and be reasonable about it. "ASAP" is not a deadline. "By Friday 14 March" is. If you need something by a date, give the date and say why it is that date, in one clause: "by Friday 14 March, because the files have to go to the shipping agent that afternoon." A reason makes the date easier to accept and easier to reschedule honestly.

Make it easy to say yes. If you want three pieces of information, list them as three numbered items rather than in a paragraph. If you want a decision between two options, write both options with their consequences, so the reply is one word rather than an essay. "Please let me know whether we ship by sea or air, as this changes the arrival date by two weeks."

Say what you have already done. If you have sent the documents twice, say so, once, without accusation: "I sent the figures on 3 and 10 March, and I am following up to see whether they reached you." That is information, not complaint.

Ask one question at the end. A single question gets a single answer. An email that asks four things gets a reply to the easiest one.

And if the answer may be no, make that easy too. "If this is not possible, please let me know by Friday and I will arrange an alternative." This gives the reader a way to decline without feeling cornered, and it is more likely to get a quick answer.
examples: Could you send me the updated figures by Friday 14 March?
Please let me know whether we ship by sea or air, as this changes the arrival date by two weeks.
If Friday is not possible, please tell me by Thursday and I will arrange an alternative.
I sent the figures on 3 and 10 March, and I am following up to see whether they reached you.
sections.heading: How to make a request

sections.body:
Two emails carry more risk than the rest: the apology and the refusal. Both are easier to get right than people think.

An apology in professional English has three parts. First, **name the fact**, plainly: "The report was sent to the wrong client." Second, **say what it cost**: "They received our internal pricing for two hours." Third, **say what you have done and what you will do**: "I have asked them to delete it, and I have checked the distribution list before sending this one." Do not explain why it happened, at least not first. A reason offered before the fact of the mistake reads as an excuse, and the reader stops reading. If there is a genuine reason, put it after the apology, in one sentence, and only if it is relevant.

Avoid the words that make an apology sound empty. "I apologise for any inconvenience caused" is a formula that says you have not thought about what happened. "We apologise for the mistake" is fine when combined with a specific account of what the mistake was. "It was a systems error" often reads as blame aimed at a system rather than at the person who pressed the button.

A refusal is easier when you refuse the request rather than the person. "I am not able to approve a budget increase of this size in this quarter" is a refusal of an action. "We are not able to take on this project this quarter, because the team is committed to the migration until May. I can give you a date in June, or a recommendation for another supplier." is better still, because it offers a next step.

Keep the refusal short. Long refusals sound apologetic, and they invite negotiation. State the decision, give the reason in one sentence, offer the alternative, close.

And be careful with softeners. "Unfortunately we are unable to proceed" is fine. "It is not that we do not want to help" is the start of an argument. Say the decision first, and then be warm about it.
examples: The report was sent to the wrong client on Monday morning. They received our internal pricing for two hours.
I have asked them to delete it, and I have checked the distribution list before sending this one.
We are not able to take on this project this quarter, because the team is committed to the migration until May.
I can give you a date in June, or a recommendation for another supplier.
sections.heading: How to apologise and how to refuse

sections.body:
**An empty subject line.** It is the most common reason a message gets lost or ignored. Write one, every time.

**A paragraph of background before the point.** The reader scrolls. Put the point in the first line and the background underneath.

**Vague deadlines.** "As soon as possible", "urgently" and "in due course" are not dates. Give the date.

**Asking three things in one email.** You will get an answer to one of them. Split the email, or number the questions so the reader can answer them one by one.

**Passive voice in a bad-news email.** "The figures were not sent" hides who was supposed to send them, and it makes the message sound evasive. "I did not send the figures" is clear and professional.

**Attaching a file called "document" or "final_final_v3".** Name the file so that it makes sense out of context, with a date and a version: "Quotation-March-2026-v2.pdf". And refer to the attachment in the body, so the reader knows what to open.
sections.heading: Six mistakes that make a work email look careless

sections.body:
Replying is where the tone of a working relationship is set. A few rules make a reply easy and quick.

**Answer the question asked.** If someone asks two questions and you answer only one, they will have to write again. If you cannot answer one, say so: "I do not have the March figures yet; I expect them by Thursday and will send them then."

**Put your answer near the top.** If the reply is long, start with a one-line summary: "Yes, we can ship by air, at a cost of $340 extra." Then the detail.

**Be brief when the situation is brief.** A short question deserves a short answer. Five lines is often better than five paragraphs, and it makes your email easy to reply to in turn.

**Do not repeat the whole thread.** Use the reply, keep the thread, and change the subject line only if the topic has genuinely changed. "RE: RE: RE:" is normal and useful.

**Use the words of the question.** If someone asks whether you can deliver on Friday, your reply should contain "Friday". Readers scan for the specific word they asked about.

Three habits that make you easy to work with. Send a holding reply when you need longer than a day: "I have this and will come back to you by Thursday." Be careful with the reply-all button, because a note meant for one person often ends up in front of everybody. And when you forward an email to someone new, add one line at the top explaining why, because they cannot see the context you can see.
examples: Yes, we can ship by air, at a cost of $340 extra.
I do not have the March figures yet; I expect them by Thursday and will send them then.
I have this and will come back to you by Thursday.
Forwarding this for your information — the deadline mentioned below still applies.
sections.heading: How to reply, and how to be brief

sections.body:
Email is also a filing system, and a badly filed email is a lost email.

**Name attachments so they survive.** Put the topic first, then the date, then the version: "Quotation-March-2026-v2.pdf". Avoid spaces if you can, because they break in some systems, and avoid names that only make sense to you. Two files called "final" and "final (2)" are not versions.

**Refer to the attachment in the body.** "Please find attached" assumes the reader can tell what it is. "I have attached the revised quotation, dated 12 March, with the delivery date changed to 28 March." tells them everything, including whether they have the right version.

**Check the recipient list against the file.** This is the mistake that ends careers: sending a document with a whole distribution list on it to a client. Before you press send, look at the top row of recipients and ask whether every one of them should see every attachment.

**Use CC for transparency, BCC for bulk.** If a colleague should see who else was contacted, CC them. If you are writing to twenty people who do not need to see each other's addresses, use BCC, or a mailing list.

**Reply to the thread, and keep the thread.** The history is the record of what was agreed. If you must start a new subject line, say in the first line that it continues an earlier conversation and quote the date.

And put anything you will need to find again where you can find it. If an agreement matters, say in the email: "As agreed in this email, we will deliver on 28 March." That one sentence turns a message into a record.
examples: I have attached the revised quotation, dated 12 March, with the delivery date changed to 28 March.
As agreed in this email, we will deliver on 28 March.
File name: Quotation-March-2026-v2.pdf
Continuing my email of 12 March about the March delivery.
sections.heading: Attachments, distribution and the record

sections.body:
Most working email is one of a small number of types, and once you recognise the type you know what shape it takes.

**The application.** The subject names the role and the date: "Application: Data Analyst, posted 14 March". One paragraph on why you are applying, one on the strongest evidence, one on availability. Attach the CV and say so. Keep it under a page.

**The follow-up.** A short email that refers to an earlier one by date. "This is a brief follow-up to my email of 12 March, and to our call on the same day." Then the ask, restated. One or two sentences of body is enough.

**The meeting request.** Name the purpose, the length, the options and the preparation. "Could we meet for 30 minutes on Tuesday or Wednesday afternoon to review the quotation? I will prepare a one-page summary." An agenda of three lines is enough for most working meetings.

**The status update.** For a colleague or a manager: what is done, what is at risk, what you need. "Completed: the supplier list. In progress: the pricing model. At risk: the delivery date, because the sea freight booking closes on Friday."

**The instruction.** To a team. What to do, by when, and what "done" looks like. Number the tasks. Say who to ask when there is a question.

**The complaint to a supplier.** Facts first, in a neutral order, with dates and quantities. Then the impact, then what you want. "The 14 March delivery did not arrive. We were told the goods would be held at customs. We need the remaining 200 units by 2 April. Please confirm today whether that is possible."

And one type that is worth knowing: the **out-of-office** reply. It should say when you are back, who to contact, and what is already handled. It is three lines, and it saves everyone a waiting email.
examples: Subject: Application — Data Analyst, posted 14 March
Completed: the supplier list. In progress: the pricing model. At risk: the delivery date.
Could we meet for 30 minutes on Tuesday or Wednesday afternoon to review the quotation?
I am away until 20 April. Please contact my colleague Mai Nguyen for anything urgent.
sections.heading: The email types you will write most

item.summary: Professional email is a written register with its own rules: a subject line that gets opened, a structure the reader can scan, and a tone that survives being read without your voice. After reading this you can write a clear request, a careful apology, a firm refusal and a follow-up, and you will know the words each of them needs.
item.title: Writing Professional Emails in English
